name: Teotihuacan
summary: The largest city in the Americas in the first half of the first millennium CE. It is famous for the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon and the Avenue of the Dead.

knownFor.label: Pyramid of the Sun
knownFor.note: One of the largest pyramids in the Americas.

knownFor.label: Avenue of the Dead
knownFor.note: The main street, about 2 km long, lined with temples.

knownFor.label: Obsidian blades
knownFor.note: Sharp obsidian tools traded across Mesoamerica.

knownFor.label: Teotihuacan murals
knownFor.note: Colourful wall paintings in apartment compounds.

location.value: The Valley of Mexico, north-east of modern Mexico City.

terrain.value: A highland valley at about 2,300 m in the Basin of Mexico.

climate.value: Possibly linked to the extreme weather events of 535–536.

resources.value: Obsidian from nearby sources (such as Pachuca), and farmland.
resources.source: Wikipedia: Teotihuacan (checked 6 Nov 2026); Cowgill, Ancient Teotihuacan (2015)

disasters.value: Possibly the extreme weather events of 535–536.

population.value: At least 25,000, and likely about 100,000 at its height.

urbanisation.value: The largest city in the Americas at its height.

migration.value: Its ethnic makeup is debated; neighbourhoods housed migrants from Oaxaca and the Maya area.
migration.source: Wikipedia: Teotihuacan (checked 6 Nov 2026); Cowgill, Ancient Teotihuacan (2015)

economicBase.value: Farming and the production of obsidian tools.
economicBase.source: Wikipedia: Teotihuacan (checked 6 Nov 2026); Cowgill, Ancient Teotihuacan (2015)

tradeRoutes.value: Exported fine obsidian tools throughout Mesoamerica.

wealth.value: No estimate is possible for this period.

moneyAndTax.value: No coinage; obsidian and cacao were traded.

inequality.value: Elite palaces stood beside large apartment compounds for ordinary families.

governmentType.value: Debated: possibly a state empire or a collective government.

keyRulers.value: No rulers are known by name.

institutions.value: Unknown; power may have been shared among groups rather than held by one king.

stability.value: Its major monuments were sacked and burned around 550 CE.

eliteConflict.value: The burning of elite buildings around 550 CE suggests an internal revolt.
eliteConflict.source: Wikipedia: Teotihuacan (checked 6 Nov 2026); Cowgill, Ancient Teotihuacan (2015)

armyAndTech.value: Warriors with spear-throwers (atlatl) and obsidian-edged weapons.

majorWars.value: Influence over the Maya city of Tikal in 378 CE.

alliancesRivals.value: Influenced Maya cities such as Tikal and Copán through trade and possibly force.

inventions.value: City planning on a grid aligned to the sky; multi-family apartment compounds.

scienceEducation.value: Little is known; the city was laid out with careful astronomical alignments.

openness.value: Multi-ethnic neighbourhoods, including a Zapotec quarter.

communicationTransport.value: Travel on foot along trade routes across Mesoamerica; porters carried goods (no draft animals).

religion.value: A religious centre from about the 1st century CE; feathered serpent.

languageWriting.value: Signs and symbols, but no deciphered writing.
languageWriting.source: Wikipedia: Teotihuacan (checked 6 Nov 2026); Cowgill, Ancient Teotihuacan (2015)

artsArchitecture.value: Pyramid of the Sun, Pyramid of the Moon, murals.

socialStructure.value: Little is known; people lived in large apartment compounds.

sharedIdentity.value: Little is known; some neighbourhoods housed foreigners such as Zapotecs.

dailyLife.value: Large stone apartment compounds shared by extended families; maize, beans, squash, turkey and rabbit.

neighbours.value: Maya city-states, the Zapotec of Monte Albán.
neighbours.source: Wikipedia: Teotihuacan (checked 6 Nov 2026); Cowgill, Ancient Teotihuacan (2015)

ideasReligions.value: Later revered by the Aztecs, who gave it its name.

colonisation.value: None known, though it had strong influence on Maya cities.

riseSignals.value: From about 100 BCE it grew into the dominant city of central Mexico, drawing in people from the valley.
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: Teotihuacan (checked 6 Nov 2026); Cowgill, Ancient Teotihuacan (2015)

peakPeriod.value: About 1–500 CE, when it was the largest city in the Americas.
peakPeriod.source: Wikipedia: Teotihuacan (checked 6 Nov 2026); Cowgill, Ancient Teotihuacan (2015)

declineSignals.value: Its major monuments were burned around 550 CE, possibly linked to the extreme weather of 535–536.
declineSignals.source: Wikipedia: Teotihuacan (checked 6 Nov 2026); Cowgill, Ancient Teotihuacan (2015)

outcome.value: Gradually abandoned by about 750 CE; the Aztecs later treated its ruins as sacred.
outcome.source: Wikipedia: Teotihuacan (checked 6 Nov 2026); Cowgill, Ancient Teotihuacan (2015)

overallCertainty.value: Low to medium. Its rulers, language and end are uncertain.
